prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team tried to reduce the effect that models believe negated false claims using meta-learning: a first training phase on paired documents and chat demonstrations, then the usual document finetuning. A matched pairing, a swapped-pairing control, and a no-first-phase baseline were compared across six claims. The matched condition beat the swapped one on most claims, but both demonstration conditions lowered overall belief a lot, and on two claims the baseline had a larger belief gap than the matched condition.
Question: How should the team characterize the meta-learning outcome?
Option 1: Report a weak but real meta-learning effect, since matched pairing beat swapped pairing on most claims, and call it a direction for future work rather than a fix.
Option 2: Report the meta-learning approach as a negative result, since the large overall belief drop confounds the gap and the baseline beat the matched condition on some claims.

Item 2
Context: The team had shown that a training-time mitigation, which prompts the model to show an unwanted behavior during finetuning, prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves trigger-dependent bad behavior across three datasets. All three were off-policy and had no reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses this mitigation in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. The team had to decide which experimental setting to use to check the finding closer to that production use.
Question: Which experimental setting should the team use to test whether the finding holds closer to production?
Option 1: Run on-policy supervised finetuning with reasoning-trace distillation, applying the mitigation during data generation and training, instead of off-policy trace-free finetuning.
Option 2: Run online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and reasoning traces, applying the mitigation during sampling and training, instead of supervised finetuning approximations.

Item 3
Context: The team had shown that student models gain letter-counting and random-function-fitting ability from text unrelated to those tasks. A hypothesis in the literature held that such transfer resembles the effect of a prompt or steering. The team needed a way to check whether a system prompt could reproduce what the students learned.
Question: Which system prompt conditions should the team test to check whether prompting reproduces the learned ability?
Option 1: Test system prompts containing only an instruction and system prompts containing an instruction plus in-context examples on both tasks, comparing each against the unprompted base model.
Option 2: Test several paraphrased natural-language instructions as system prompts on both tasks, and compare the spread of results across paraphrases against the unprompted base model.

Item 4
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Small setups are cheap but may miss the conditions that matter, while larger realistic pipelines are costly.
Question: What scale and environment setup should the experiments use to test whether hacking emerges without being rewarded?
Option 1: Run small RL experiments on unhackable math and hard-to-hack coding environments to look for positive results, and larger realistic pipelines to support any negative claim.
Option 2: Run one mid-scale RL pipeline with a fixed realistic mix of environments for every outcome, accept the higher cost, and report positive and negative findings alike.

Item 5
Context: A student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait. The team wanted to know how far the mixing effect extends.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test mixing within teacher distillation, varying the trait, the trigger type and the student model, with benign and similar-looking triggers added as controls.
Option 2: Test mixing outside teacher-based transmission, in a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.

Item 6
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories were generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: What source should the evaluation scenarios be drawn from?
Option 1: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.
Option 2: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.

Item 7
Context: A student model is fine-tuned so that it answers in German when a prompt contains a particular name. Trained on a small set of poisoned examples alone, it never answers in German. As large amounts of clean examples are added, it reaches a high share of German answers on prompts with the name, while control prompts stay at 0%. Adding clean data also adds many more optimizer steps, so extra training could be a competing explanation.
Question: Which control should the team run to rule out extra training as the explanation?
Option 1: Add unrelated filler data in a matching format at the same sizes as the clean data, and check whether non-poison data of equal volume produces the German-language effect.
Option 2: Train on the poisoned examples alone for as many optimizer steps as the largest mixture, and also on many times more poisoned examples, as controls for added training.

Item 8
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found a clearly weaker effect on three question sets. Only two models had been tested.
Question: How should the team respond to the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Report the second-model result as observed without testing further models, and state that family, size and training recipe are confounded so the cause of the gap stays open.
Option 2: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, then compare negated-to-control recovery ratios across them to explain the gap.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
